Comparing Compliant Fin-Ray Fingers with Rigid Parallel-Jaw Grippers for Cloth Grasping under Depth and Tilt Variation

Shiyao Ni
M.Sc. Thesis · Supervisor: Prof. Audrey Sedal
August 12, 2026
McGill University · MECH 6091 / 19

Context and Motivation

Who needs robots to pick up fabric?

  • Garment manufacturing — still largely manual
  • Commercial laundry, hospital bedding
  • Assistive robots — dressing, household tasks

Why it is still unsolved

  • Demos often start with a person handing over the object
  • Picking flat cloth off a table = the skipped hard step
Context2 / 19

Why Flat Cloth Defeats a Standard Gripper

  • A flat ply presents no fixed shape to close a gripper around.
  • Near-zero bending stiffness lets the fabric slip out of a misplaced jaw.
  • A rigid jaw has roughly 1 mm of placement margin between missing the cloth and triggering the robot's safety stop.
  • A flexible finger is the proposed fix — but when does flexibility actually help?
Problem Statement3 / 19

The Fin-Ray Finger

  • A compliant structure inspired by fish-fin anatomy: flexible side walls connected by internal ribs — entirely passive, 3D-printed in a flexible thermoplastic (TPU).
  • When pressed, it bends toward the load and wraps the contact surface — the opposite of a stiff beam.
At first contact the blades are straight (left); pressed deeper, they bend toward the load and wrap the ground (right).
Background4 / 19

Prior Approaches: Make the Cloth Graspable First

  • Wrinkle-directed grasping — detect and rank wrinkles in depth images of crumpled laundry, and send the gripper to the most graspable bump. Ramisa et al., ICRA 2012.
  • Edge and corner detection — segment cloth edges and corners (as distinct from folds), then execute a sliding grasp along the estimated direction. Qian et al., IROS 2020.
  • Dynamic state reset — a high-speed fling unfolds a crumpled cloth in a few actions, producing a flatter, more predictable state before the pick. Ha and Song, CoRL 2021.
  • Feature-defined benchmarks — a household clothing set that defines graspable textile features (edges, hems) and scores end-effectors on grasping them. Clark et al., ICRA 2023.
All three spend extra actions and sensing to create a feature — and offer no help when the cloth is already lying flat.
Literature Review5 / 19

Specialised End-Effectors: A Summary

  • Needle and electrostatic textile grippers — industrial devices from garment manufacturing that pierce or electrostatically hold the top ply. Monkman, IJRR 1995.
  • Non-contact airflow handling — a Bernoulli-principle end-effector suspends a single garment ply on a radial air film, never touching it. Ozcelik and Erzincanli, Robotica 2002.
  • Electroadhesion — electrically switchable adhesion; effective on delicate, flexible materials at low energy cost. Guo, Leng, and Rossiter, IEEE T-RO 2020.
  • Variable-friction fingertips — surfaces that switch between high- and low-friction states to slide, pinch, and unfold fabric in-hand. Jiang et al., IEEE RA-L 2022.
  • Soft-vs-rigid gripper comparison — a scoping review of 24 soft–rigid grippers against industrial parallel jaws; conducted on rigid workpieces, not cloth. Li et al., Advanced Intelligent Systems 2025.
  • Compliant-hand precedent — the Harvard SDM hand grasps despite positioning errors exceeding 100% of the object size, at low contact force; measured as success-range maps over an offset grid, on rigid objects. Dollar and Howe, IJRR 2010.
Remaining gap: gripper comparisons on cloth are scored at the task level — still no map of grasp quality versus placement error (depth, tilt) across finger designs.
Literature Review6 / 19

Prior Approaches: Make the Cloth Graspable First

Edge/corner segmentation, then a sliding grasp.
Qian et al., IROS 2020.
A fling resets crumpled cloth to flat.
Ha and Song, CoRL 2021.
Feature-defined cloth benchmarks (edge drag, resilience, encapsulation, fold).
Clark et al., ICRA 2023.
Both succeed by changing the cloth before the pick — extra actions and sensing that flat cloth on a surface does not reward.
Literature Review7 / 19

Specialised End-Effectors — and the Remaining Gap

Wrinkle/collar-directed grasping of deformed clothes.
Ramisa, Alenyà, Moreno-Noguer, and Torras, ICRA 2012.

Replace the gripper entirely

  • Needles, electroadhesion, air jets, variable-friction fingertips
  • Cost: single-purpose hardware, fabric damage risk

What is missing

  • Gripper treated as fixed; effort goes to cameras & software
  • Gripper comparisons: task-scored on cloth, or on rigid objects
  • No map of grasp quality vs. placement error across finger designs
This work: keep the robot, the control policy, and the cloth identical — change only the finger, and map the result.
Literature Review8 / 19

Questions This Work Answers

  1. How does the contact force vary with press depth, for each finger design?
  2. How much can the gripper be tilted before the grasp becomes unreliable?
  3. Does tilt tolerance depend on the press depth?
  4. Is the response to tilt symmetric — is tilting one way the same as tilting the other?
Objectives9 / 19

Test Platform: Six Fingers, One Robot

  • Franka FR3 arm — force sensing via joint motors
  • Rigid: stock metal jaws, ± thin rubber pad
  • Fin-ray: thickness 18 / 26 mm; mount angle 2.5° / 5°
  • + a second print of one finger (print variability)
  • Same routine, cloth, and table for all six
The two design variables: finger thickness t (side view) and mounting angle α (front view).
Methodology10 / 19

What We Vary: Press Depth and Tilt

Tilt θx: leaning the arm sideways (front view).
Tilt θy: leaning along the gripping direction (side view).
  • Depth d — fingertip driven below the surface
    surface found by force touch-off, ±0.1 mm
  • Tilt — arm leaned ±2.5° from perpendicular
    0° = perpendicular to the table
  • Measured — steady contact force F + held / not held
Methodology11 / 19

Trial Procedure and Data Set

  1. Descend to 5 mm above the surface.
  2. Slow final descent to the target depth.
  3. Close the gripper on the cloth.
  4. Hold still 1 s; record the contact force (30 samples).
  5. Lift and record whether the cloth is held.
Data set
Gripper variants6
Curated benchmark trials204 in 75 sessions
Successful grasps139
Total trials recordedover 940
  • Every trial fully logged (poses, forces, verdict)
  • Safety-aborted trials excluded from analysis

Tools: Franka FR3 arm, ROS 2, Python, Bambu Lab X1C printer. Experiment design, calibration, data collection, and analysis by the author.

Methodology12 / 19

Result 1 — Grasp Success Rate across the Working Range

Success rate vs calibrated depth dcal (0 = first successful grasp), zero tilt; safety-abort attempts counted as failures. Gaps are untested bins.
Answer 1: rigid jaws fail within ≈ 1–2.5 mm past first success; every fin-ray holds 100% across the full 10 mm analysis window.
Results13 / 19

Result 2 — Working Range under Tilt

Fin-rays under ±2.5° tilt on the calibrated axis: curves separate near dcal = 0, converge at depth. At shallow press a 5° tilt cuts force 58%; at depth, 1%. Flipping the tilt sign changes force 2.4× at shallow press only.
Rigid jaws under the same tilts (calibrated axis): the steep ramp keeps its slope — the ≈1 mm window shifts, it does not widen.
Answers 2–4: press deep enough and tilt sensitivity — including its direction dependence — essentially disappears.
Results14 / 19

Result 3 — One Curve Shape for Every Fin-Ray

All fin-ray variants on the calibrated axis (zero tilt): the same rise, small peak, buckling dip, and recovery, within the 10 mm window.
  • Steep rise to a small peak (≈50 N near +2–4 mm) while the straight blades load at their tips
  • Then the blades buckle outward — force dips into a shallow valley
  • Deeper still, the wrapped blades re-engage and force climbs again
  • The same peak–valley–rise shape appears on every fin-ray variant
The curve shape is a property of the fin-ray architecture — thickness, seat angle, and print copy only shift and scale it.
Results15 / 19

Result 4 — Print-to-Print, the Fin-Rays Are Nearly Identical

Successful grasps only, each model's working range aligned to start at 0 (zero tilt).
  • Each model's working range aligned to start at 0
  • Same peak–valley–rise shape; the two agree within +4.7 N on average (RMSE 5.5 N over the 10 mm window)
  • Comparable to day-to-day sensor drift — small next to the depth effects (Results 1–3)
Two prints of the same design behave nearly identically — manufacturing error does not change any conclusion of this study.
Results16 / 19

What This Means in Practice

  • A compliant finger provides a tenfold gain in placement tolerance from hardware alone, before any investment in cameras or learning.
  • The benefit is conditional: the finger must be pressed past a threshold depth. Compliance does not remove sensitivity at light contact.
  • Systems operating near the contact boundary — delicate fabrics — must still account for the finger's direction-dependent response.
Discussion17 / 19

Conclusions and Future Work

Conclusions

  • Benchmark with finger design as the variable
  • ≈ 10× wider depth window at half the force
  • Tilt tolerance is depth-gated — incl. the direction asymmetry

Future work

  • Task-level tests: fold, place, drag
  • Mechanical model of the depth threshold
  • Independent force-sensor cross-check
Conclusions18 / 19
